# Process cooling water cleaning, flushing and passivation — Tull Creek Data Hall, turnover package

You are the commissioning engineer for the flushing contractor on a new data hall. The project
document library for this task is the directory tree around this file: `drawings/` (P&ID and
isometric sheets, site logistics and the temporary power single line, DXF, plan units are feet),
`schedules/` (pipe, equipment, valve and tie-in schedules, XLSX), `specs/` (the project
specification sections, DOCX), `standards/` (the public standards and criteria documents the
specification adopts, PDF), `site/` (construction water, the water analysis, the discharge
authorisation and temporary power, DOCX / PDF / XLSX), `vendor_data/` (reviewed submittals and a
priced chemical quotation, PDF / XLSX), `commissioning/` (turnover milestones, the hydrostatic test
record and a checklist template, XLSX / CSV) and `correspondence/` (RFI responses). Not every
document is relevant, and the information you need is spread across them: read the project
specification first and let it tell you which documents govern what.

Some documents in the library are **scanned images with no text layer**. Their contents cannot be
extracted as text and must be read as images; do not conclude that a document is empty or
irrelevant because text extraction returns nothing.

## Situation

The Process Cooling Water (PCW) loop is mechanically complete. It is divided into eight
tie-in-bounded circuits of different sizes, metallurgies and hold-up volumes. Before turnover every
circuit must be flushed, chemically cleaned, rinsed, passivated and filled with its treatment
programme, and the whole campaign must be executed with a fixed rented fleet of flush skids, a
metered construction-water allocation, a single authorised sewer discharge point, the temporary
power available at each tie-in, two commissioning crews and a contractual turnover date.

Which lines belong to which circuit is shown on the drawings, not tabulated anywhere. The rest of
the engineering is yours: the flow each circuit must be flushed at and whether the skid you assign
can deliver it against that circuit's head; the treatment programme each circuit's metallurgy and
the site's makeup water admit; how much product that needs and how long the passivation film must be
held; how many rinse displacements it takes to reach the acceptance criterion; whether rinse water
can be cascaded from one circuit to another; where each discharge goes; and how all of that fits the
water, fleet, power, discharge and schedule limits at the lowest total programme cost.

## Deliverable

Produce `output/submission.zip` containing the seven files below. **The schema is a contract, not
part of the problem: every column and every stage token you need is listed here.** Column names are
matched case-insensitively and `_`, `-` and space are equivalent; common synonyms are accepted, and
extra columns of your own are ignored. Rows may be in any order. Use these stage tokens:

    HYDRO   INITIAL_FLUSH   CHEM_CLEAN   DRAIN_RINSE   PASSIVATE   HOLD   FINAL_FILL

You may add activities of your own (set-up, strainer removal, demobilisation); they are ignored, not
penalised. A stage token that cannot be resolved costs the package family; and if the stage it was
meant to be was one of the seven above, the circuit also loses every family that needed that stage —
an unreadable token does not stand in for the stage it was meant to name.

One cell value is fatal, and only in one place. In the numeric columns the grader reads — `flow_gpm`,
`velocity_fps`, `reynolds`, `required_head_ft`, `skid_head_avail_ft`, `duration_h`,
`circuit_volume_gal`, `system_volume_gal`, `passes`, `water_volume_gal`, `discharge_volume_gal`,
`discharge_ph`, `discharge_temp_f`, `target_ppm`, `product_quantity`, `basis_volume_gal`,
`ph_target_lo`, `ph_target_hi`, `threshold_value`, `start_h`, `finish_h` — a cell reading `TBD`,
`TBA`, `to be determined`, `to be advised`, `NaN`, `Inf`, `XXX` or `<fill in>` scores the whole
package zero: a placeholder
is not an answer — in any of the four plan CSVs, on any row. In any other column, including every
column of your own, those words are ignored. `--`, `N/A`, `NONE` and an empty cell are ordinary
"not applicable" everywhere and are never penalised, so a column a row does not use (the skid and
flow columns on `HYDRO` and `HOLD`, the test pressure off the hydrostatic row) should be left blank
or set to one of those rather than to `TBD`.

The rented fleet is a closed vocabulary: `skid_id` on a pumped row must name one or more of the
three units on hire, `+`-joined. Case, spaces, hyphens and underscores are equivalent. A cell that
names anything else — a model rather than a unit, a unit that was never hired, or nothing at all —
costs the skid-fleet family for the programme; it never makes the package unreadable.

`HYDRO` and `HOLD` are not pumped stages: on those rows the skid, flow, velocity, Reynolds and head
columns do not apply and may be left blank or set to `NONE`. `HYDRO` carries its test pressure and
its duration; `HOLD` carries only its duration. Every other stage carries the full row. A circuit
whose hydrostatic test is already on record as accepted needs no `HYDRO` row; if you file one for
it, give it a duration of zero and no water, and it is read as a test not performed.

1. `flush_plan.csv` — one row per circuit and stage. Columns:
   `circuit_id` · `stage` · `skid_id` (the rented unit ids, `+`-joined if more than one) ·
   `skids_parallel` (count) · `flow_gpm` · `governing_segment` (line number) ·
   `governing_id_in` (in.) · `velocity_fps` (ft/s) · `reynolds` · `required_head_ft` (ft w.c.) ·
   `skid_head_avail_ft` (ft w.c.) · `duration_h` (the scheduled occupancy, hours) ·
   `circuit_volume_gal` (the FLUSH volume) · `system_volume_gal` · `passes` (displacements, on the
   flush and rinse rows) · `water_source` (`MAKEUP`, or `CASCADE_FROM:<circuit>`) ·
   `water_volume_gal` · `discharge_route` (`SEWER`, `HAUL` or `NONE`) · `discharge_volume_gal` ·
   `discharge_ph` · `discharge_temp_f` (degF) · `test_pressure_psig` (on the hydrostatic row) ·
   `protection` (the temporary bypasses and strainer fitted for that stage) ·
   `turnover_method` (the method the project specification permits at turnover).
2. `chemistry_plan.csv` — one row per circuit, stage and product. Columns:
   `circuit_id` · `stage` · `program` (the treatment programme, on the treatment rows) ·
   `product_id` · `active_species` · `target_ppm` · `basis_volume_gal` (the volume the dose is
   referred to) · `product_quantity` · `product_unit` · `packages` (whole packages) ·
   `ph_target_lo` · `ph_target_hi` · `hold_days` · `source_doc` · `source_clause`.
   A roll-up row whose stage is an order total is ignored.
3. `acceptance_matrix.csv` — one row per circuit, gate and parameter. Columns:
   `circuit_id` · `gate` · `parameter` · `method` · `sample_point_tag` ·
   `threshold_op` (`>=`/`<=`, or `lower limit`/`upper limit`) · `threshold_value` · `units` ·
   `basis_doc` · `basis_clause`. The gates and parameters the turnover log must carry are listed in
   the project specification; the grader matches a row by its gate and the quantity named in its
   parameter, not by an exact spelling.
4. `schedule.csv` — one row per activity; a stage may be split into several. Columns:
   `activity_id` · `circuit_id` · `stage` · `predecessor_ids` · `start_h` · `finish_h` (hours from
   mobilisation) · `skid_id` · `crew_id` · `water_draw_gal`.
5. `resources.json` — an object with `skid_assignment`, `water_profile`, `discharge_profile`,
   `power_check`, `chemical_orders` and `cost`. `chemical_orders` is a list of objects carrying at
   least `product_id`, `packages`, `lead_days` and `order_by_day` (days from mobilisation; negative
   means before it). `cost` carries the breakdown and a total under `total_usd`.
6. `constraint_register.csv` — columns `id, document, clause, requirement, value, items_bound`:
   every requirement you applied, each with the document and clause or table it comes from, the
   value you used and what it binds. Cite the real project documents and clauses, not this brief.
   The register is scored on recall of the requirements the grader checks (at least 90 % of the hard
   requirements must be present, matched on document plus clause) and on value agreement; extra
   correct rows are neutral and there is no cap on the number of rows, and **a hard requirement
   missing from the register makes every family it governs count as not passed**. Rows citing a
   superseded, cancelled or non-adopted document as their authority count against you: **a single
   such row fails the register family**. Recording that a document is superseded while citing the
   current one, or citing a standard an adopted document itself invokes, is not such a row.
   **The register lists only the requirements you applied.** A row whose `document` cell names a
   superseded, cancelled or non-adopted document is a row citing that document as its authority
   **whatever its requirement or value text says** — writing "out of scope", "not applied" or
   "reviewed and rejected" in another column does not make it a different row. Record the documents
   you read and rejected, and why, in `MOP.md`, not in the register.
7. `MOP.md` — the Method of Procedure: the execution narrative **and** the design basis. The design
   basis must give, for each circuit, **the governing constraint and its margin**. The governing
   constraint is whichever of these five your own plan leaves the least room against — the flushing
   duty against the head the assigned skid can deliver; the rinse endpoint; the authorised programme
   discharge volume; the site's daily water allocation; the temporary power available at the tie-in
   — and the margin is the fractional room left, `(limit − achieved) / limit`, as a decimal. Name
   one per circuit and state its margin. Some of these margins can be written in more than one
   quantity — the rinse in displacements or in the quantity its endpoint is measured in — and they
   are genuinely different numbers; **every form the project specification permits counts, and which
   constraint binds is decided using whichever permitted form of each is the tighter**, so a
   constraint that is tightest in any permitted quantity is a defensible answer. The rinse margin may be
   given either in displacements or in whatever quantity the acceptance
   criterion you are working to is expressed in. Which one binds, and by how much, is yours to
   work out; record the resolution of every conflict you found between the
   project documents, the margins and judgement calls you made, the defects you found, and a safety
   section discharging the chemical-handling obligations of the standard the specification adopts
   for hazard communication.

Every number you report must agree with the plan it describes: the figures that are scored are
recomputed from your flows, passes, routes, methods and schedule, not taken from your columns.
The rinse is the one exception for the effluent columns: its effluent runs from the spent
cleaning solution to the makeup water over the displacements, so any `discharge_ph` and
`discharge_temp_f` inside the acceptance band the discharge authorisation states is accepted on
a `DRAIN_RINSE` row.

The project specification states how water, effluent, attended time and cost are accounted, and what
the turnover options are. Follow it: the plan is priced on that basis.

## How the package is assessed

The plan is checked circuit by circuit against the requirements of the project documents, and the
programme is credited for its total cost against the lowest cost the documents allow: a cheaper
programme scores higher. Each circuit scores 0.4·p² + 0.6·h⁴·O, where p is the fraction of its 24
constraint families that count, h the fraction of its 20 hard families that count (a family counts
when the circuit passes it and the register carries the hard requirements that govern it), and O is
the lowest cost the documents allow divided by the cost of your programme, at most 1. A hard failure
does not withhold O; it discounts it through h⁴. The task score is the mean over the graded circuits.
A circuit whose rows are missing or unparseable scores 0.

Work from the documents. Where they leave something to the engineer, decide and record it in the
design basis.


## Verifier access (blind variant)

No verifier, oracle, or evaluation data of any kind is available in this workspace — the
only checks you can run are the ones you build yourself. Work from the brief and the
documents alone and submit your best final deliverable; it will be graded offline by the
frozen verifier on held-out instances.
I'll start by exploring the project structure and reading the task file.

[Title] SECTION 23 25 16 - PROCESS COOLING WATER CLEANING, FLUSHING AND PASSIVATION
[Normal] Tull Creek Data Hall - Issued for Construction, Rev 3, 2026-07-14
[Heading 2] 1.1   SUMMARY
[Normal] This Section covers pre-operational cleaning, flushing, chemical cleaning, passivation and turnover of the Process Cooling Water (PCW) system, circuit by circuit.
[Normal] The PCW system is a closed process cooling water loop. Apply the closed-system provisions of the governing water-treatment criteria document; the provisions written for open recirculating cooling-tower systems do not apply to this system except where this Section invokes them explicitly.
[Normal] Where this Section and the governing water-treatment criteria document both address a subject, the more restrictive requirement governs.
[Heading 2] 1.2   GOVERNING DOCUMENTS
[Normal] UFC 3-230-13, Industrial Water Treatment Operation and Maintenance (current edition). The 2005 edition, UFC 3-240-13FN, is cancelled and must not be used.
[Normal] DOE-HDBK-1012/3-92, Thermodynamics, Heat Transfer and Fluid Flow, Volume 3, for all hydraulic relations.
[Normal] 40 CFR 403, General Pretreatment Regulations, for discharge to the publicly owned treatment works.
[Normal] 29 CFR 1910.1200, Hazard Communication, for all products brought on site.
[Normal] Section 23 21 16 for pipe materials, roughness and the hydrostatic test regime.
[Heading 2] 1.5   FLUSHING, TESTING AND WATER-TREATMENT LOG
[Normal] Maintain and submit a log recording, for every circuit: the minimum flushing velocity achieved and the segment at which it was measured; the temporary strainer mesh and its removal milestone; the chemical cleaning circulation time; the rinse water test results (clarity, suspended solids, conductivity and pH) against the makeup water; the passivation inhibitor residual, pH and film-formation hold duration; and every discharge event with its volume, route, pH and temperature. Use the form of CX-03.
[Normal] Submit with the log an acceptance matrix stating, for every circuit, the acceptance threshold applied at each gate, with the document and clause it comes from. The matrix must carry at least the following, each with the sense and the numeric value of its threshold:
[Normal]   a. RINSE gate: conductivity (upper limit), pH (lower limit and upper limit);
[Normal]   b. PASSIVATION gate: the inhibitor residual at the start of film formation (lower limit);
[Normal]   c. DISCHARGE gate: pH (lower limit) and temperature (upper limit) at the authorised discharge point;
[Normal]   d. TURNOVER gate: the maintenance inhibitor residual (lower limit) and the total aerobic bacteria count (upper limit), both to the limits of the governing water-treatment criteria document.
[Heading 2] 1.6   DESIGN BASIS AND METHOD OF PROCEDURE
[Normal] Submit a Method of Procedure (MOP) containing the execution narrative and the design basis.
[Normal] Where a constraint can be expressed in more than one quantity - the rinse, for instance, in displacements or in conductivity - the margin may be stated in ANY of them; state which.
[Normal] The design basis must state, for each circuit, a line of exactly the form
[Normal]     GOVERNING CONSTRAINT <circuit>: <constraint family> (margin <value>)
[Normal] where <constraint family> is the constraint family that is binding for that circuit and <value> is its relative margin, that is (limit - achieved)/limit for an upper limit and (achieved - limit)/limit for a lower limit, as a decimal fraction.
[Normal] The design basis must also record the resolution of every conflict found between the project documents, the margins applied, and the defects found in the documents.
[Heading 2] 3.2   HYDRAULIC BASIS
[Normal] Compute every hydraulic quantity by the relations of DOE-HDBK-1012/3-92 with the following project conventions. Design flush water properties: density 62.30 lbm/ft3, kinematic viscosity 1.08e-5 ft2/s at 68 degF.
[Normal] For DOSING arithmetic - converting a target residual in parts per million to a mass of active species - use a water density of 8.34 lb/gal. A residual of 1 ppm in 1,000 gallons is therefore 0.00834 lb of the active species.
[Normal] a. Velocity in a leg is v = Q_leg / A, where Q_leg is that leg's share of the circuit flow and A is the inside cross-sectional area from Schedule M-601. Parallel legs of one line carry an equal share.
[Normal] b. Friction factor from the Colebrook-White relation, solved iteratively:
[Normal]        1/sqrt(f) = -2 log10( (e/D)/3.7 + 2.51/(Re sqrt(f)) )
[Normal]    with absolute roughness e from Section 23 21 16 and Re = v D / nu. Below Re 2000 use f = 64/Re.
[Normal] c. Head loss in a run is the Darcy loss over the straight length PLUS the equivalent length of its fittings, L_eq = (sum L/D) x D, with sum L/D from Schedule M-601:
[Normal]        h = f ((L + L_eq)/D) v^2 / (2 g)
[Normal] d. The required head of a circulation set is the sum of: the static lift from the tie-in to the circuit high point (isometrics M-ISO-2xx); the head loss of the MAIN circulation path, that is the lines shown on M-601 with a single leg, at the total circuit flow; the pressure drop of every component left in the flushed path, scaled as dP_rated x (Q/Q_rated)^2 from Schedule M-602; and, for EACH skid separately at that skid's own share of the flow, the head loss of its temporary hose run and the pressure drop of its temporary strainer, scaled as dP_rated x (Q_skid/Q_rated)^2 from VD-05.
[Normal] e. Where two or more skids are used on one circuit they are connected in parallel: they share the total flow equally and each must develop the required head at its own flow, per DOE-HDBK-1012/3-92.
[Normal] f. A duty point beyond the last point of a published pump curve is not acceptable.
[Heading 2] 3.3   FLUSHING VELOCITY
[Normal] The flushing flow of a circuit shall be not less than the flow required to achieve, in EVERY leg of EVERY line of that circuit, the greater of:
[Normal]   a. the water velocity that the governing water-treatment criteria document requires for keeping foulants in suspension; and
[Normal]   b. the project minimum for the circuit's velocity class, namely 4.0 ft/s for any circuit that serves a plate heat exchanger or a cold-plate device, and 2.0 ft/s otherwise.
[Normal] The flushing flow shall be maintained through the initial flush, the chemical cleaning circulation and every rinse displacement.
[Normal] NUMBER OF INITIAL FLUSH DISPLACEMENTS. Not fewer than ONE full circuit displacement before the cleaning charge is made up. More may be used where the Contractor judges the construction debris warrants it; the water, effluent and attended time of every displacement declared are accounted under cl.3.9 and cl.3.10 and are the Contractor's cost.
[Normal] Record in the log the segment at which the velocity is lowest; that segment is the governing segment of the circuit.
[Heading 2] 3.4   CHEMICAL CLEANING
[Normal] Clean each circuit with the cleaning product scheduled for its metallurgy in VD-06, at the application rate stated there, referred to the SYSTEM volume of the circuit (pipework plus the hold-up of every component of the circuit, whether or not it is bypassed for flushing).
[Normal] The cleaning product is dosed on that VOLUMETRIC application rate, not to a target residual: state the basis volume and the quantity of product, and leave the target residual not applicable on a cleaning row (VD-06 Note 4a).
[Normal] Carry the polymer dispersant of the governing water-treatment criteria document with the cleaning charge, at the active dosage that document states for keeping foulants in suspension.
[Normal] Circulate the cleaning solution for not less than the circulation time the governing water-treatment criteria document requires, then drain, flush and clean all strainers.
[Normal] That circulation time is CONTACT TIME and is measured in OCCUPIED HOURS: it is the sum of the hours of the activities scheduled for the stage, and an idle gap between two of them is not contact time (cl.3.10 b).
[Normal] Protect every component listed in M-602 as having a temporary bypass provision by fitting that bypass for the initial flush and the chemical cleaning. A component left in the flushed path must be shown to be within the maximum allowable pressure drop, the maximum temperature and the maximum particle size that M-602 gives it, at the declared flow.
[Heading 2] 3.5   PASSIVATION AND TREATMENT PROGRAM
[Normal] Select the closed-system treatment program from the governing water-treatment criteria document for the circuit's metallurgy and for the makeup water analysis SW-02, and maintain the residual and pH that document specifies for the program selected.
[Normal] Where that document's programme SELECTION TABLE and the controlling paragraph text of the individual programmes differ as to which programme suits a metallurgy, the paragraph text of the programme governs. The selection table is organised by system type, not by metallurgy, and does not restrict a programme to the system types it happens to list.
[Normal] Where that document tabulates a quantity in more than one table, the tables it identifies for PASSIVATION govern for passivation dosages, pH bands and film-formation times; a table written for a different duty does not.
[Normal] Passivate with the inhibitor technology that document tabulates for passivation, at a residual inside the tabulated dosage band and a pH inside the tabulated pH band, and hold the film-formation period that the CURRENT edition of that document tabulates.
[Normal] That hold, like every other required period of this Section, is measured in OCCUPIED HOURS (cl.3.10 b).
[Normal] Dose all treatment chemicals on the SYSTEM volume of the circuit.
[Normal] Where copper is wetted anywhere in the circuit, carry the azole at not less than the residual the governing document requires.
[Heading 2] 3.6   RINSE DISPLACEMENT MODEL
[Normal] The number of rinse displacements required after chemical cleaning shall be computed from the project displacement model:
[Normal]        C_n = C_mk + (C_0 - C_mk) exp(-eta n)
[Normal] where C_n is the circuit water conductivity after n full circuit-volume displacements, C_mk is the makeup water conductivity from SW-02, C_0 is the conductivity of the spent cleaning solution from VD-06, n is the number of displacements of the circuit FLUSH volume (pipework plus the hold-up of components that are NOT bypassed), and eta is the mixing efficiency of the circuit:
[Normal]        eta = 0.45 for a circuit that contains a parallel cold-plate manifold bank or coil bank, that is, a circuit any of whose components Schedule M-602 describes as a cold-plate manifold bank or a coil bank
[Normal]        eta = 0.62 for every other circuit
[Normal] n shall be a whole number of displacements, and shall be large enough that C_n satisfies the rinse acceptance criterion of the governing water-treatment criteria document.
[Normal] That criterion states the rinse pH as a tolerance and as a window in one sentence. BOTH readings are acceptable to this project: a pH limit filed either as the tolerance about the makeup pH of SW-02 or as the absolute window the document names satisfies cl.1.5, and a control band inside their intersection satisfies both.
[Normal] Each displacement takes the time the declared flow needs to move the circuit FLUSH volume, and that time too is measured in OCCUPIED HOURS (cl.3.10 b).
[Normal] A displacement may be made with the final rinse effluent of another circuit that has already satisfied the rinse acceptance criterion (a cascade). A cascaded displacement counts as a full displacement. No circuit may receive more than one cascaded displacement, and the donor circuit's rinse must be complete before the cascade begins.
[Heading 2] 3.7   DISCHARGE
[Normal] All flush, cleaning and rinse effluent shall be discharged to the metered sanitary sewer connection authorised in SW-03, or removed from site by tanker to a permitted disposal facility, at the rates quoted in SW-01 and RFI-031.
[Normal] Effluent shall meet the general pretreatment prohibitions of 40 CFR 403 and the local limits of SW-03. Any effluent stream containing a constituent for which SW-03 states a local limit that the stream cannot meet shall be hauled off site.
[Normal] The programme total authorised at the metered connection shall not be exceeded.
[Heading 2] 3.8   TURNOVER
[Normal] Bring each circuit to the maintenance residual and pH of the selected treatment program by ONE of the two methods below, at the Contractor's option. Declare the method used for each circuit in the plan, as turnover_method. Then recirculate for not less than the period the governing water-treatment criteria document requires before sampling, and sample while circulating.
[Normal]   RETAIN_AND_TOP_UP - the passivation charge is retained in the circuit and the circuit is topped up to its SYSTEM volume with treated makeup water carrying the maintenance charge. Permitted only where the maintenance residual of the selected program is not below its passivation residual, so that the top-up raises rather than dilutes the inhibitor level.
[Normal]   DRAIN_AND_REFILL - the passivation charge is drained to the route declared for it and the circuit is refilled to its SYSTEM volume with treated makeup water carrying the maintenance charge.
[Normal] REPORTING CONVENTION. On every chemistry row, target_ppm is the ABSOLUTE residual the circuit is to be held at, and product_quantity is the quantity the dose ADDS. Under RETAIN_AND_TOP_UP those differ: the top-up adds only the difference between the maintenance residual and the residual the retained charge already carries. Either the absolute quantity or the increment is accepted, provided the basis volume is stated.
[Normal] Where two tabulated inhibitors are carried at once - an inhibitor and a copper azole, for instance - and their tabulated pH bands overlap only in part, control to the INTERSECTION of the two bands, which satisfies both.
[Heading 2] 3.9   WATER AND EFFLUENT ACCOUNTING
[Normal] Account the water drawn and the effluent produced by each circuit as follows, where V_f is the circuit FLUSH volume, V_s its SYSTEM volume, n_f the number of initial flush displacements, n_r the number of rinse displacements and c is 1 if one displacement is cascaded in and 0 otherwise. State both figures for every stage in the plan.
[Normal]     hydrostatic test (where one is owed)   draw V_f              effluent V_f
[Normal]     initial flush                          draw n_f x V_f        effluent n_f x V_f
[Normal]     chemical cleaning                      draw V_f              effluent V_f
[Normal]     rinse                                  draw (n_r - c) x V_f  effluent (n_r - 1) x V_f - d
[Normal]     passivation charge                     draw 0                effluent 0
[Normal]     film-formation hold                    draw 0                effluent 0
[Normal]     turnover, RETAIN_AND_TOP_UP            draw V_s - V_f        effluent 0
[Normal]     turnover, DRAIN_AND_REFILL             draw V_s              effluent V_f
[Normal] The circuit is left FULL at the end of the last rinse displacement, so that displacement is not drained: that is why the rinse effluent is one displacement less than the rinse draw.
[Normal] The passivation charge is dosed into the water standing in the circuit at the end of the rinse; it is not a fresh fill.
[Normal] A rinse that takes one cascaded displacement and draws the rest from the metered supply is a single row with a single water_source: declare it CASCADE_FROM:<donor circuit>. The makeup balance above already accounts for the other displacements being drawn fresh.
[Normal] d is the volume this circuit DONATES to a cascade: a cascade transfers exactly one receiver displacement volume, that is the FLUSH volume of the receiving circuit, out of the donor's final rinse effluent, so the donor's effluent falls by that volume and the receiver's draw falls by the same volume. A circuit may donate to at most one receiver and receive from at most one donor, and a donor's FLUSH volume must be not less than its receiver's, or it cannot fill it.
[Normal] These figures balance: over the programme, water drawn equals effluent produced plus the SYSTEM volume left standing in every circuit at turnover.
[Normal] Water drawn by an activity that spans midnight is counted against each calendar day in proportion to the hours of the activity in that day (SW-01 cl.2).
[Heading 2] 3.10   COST BASIS
[Normal] Price the programme on the following basis, and report the total and its breakdown in the plan.
[Normal]   a. Skid rental: the fleet is on HIRE TO THE PROGRAMME, not to a circuit. Each rented unit is charged ONE day rate (SW-01 cl.3, VD-01, VD-02) for every CALENDAR DAY on which it is held anywhere on the works, counted ONCE however many circuits it serves that day. A calendar day is the period [24k, 24k+24) hours from mobilisation, k = 0, 1, 2 ... A unit is held on a day if any scheduled activity that declares it overlaps that day; a unit released for the film-formation hold is not held during it. APPORTIONMENT: divide each unit-day between the circuits that held that unit that day IN PROPORTION TO THE HOURS each held it inside the day, merging any overlap within a circuit. The share so obtained is a real number and is NOT rounded; the whole day is charged once and divided. Two circuits that share a unit-day therefore pay a part each, and a circuit whose work is spread thinly across many days pays for every one of them.
[Normal]   b. Commissioning crew: a crew is ENGAGED BY THE SHIFT, not by the circuit. Each crew is charged ONE shift rate for every 12-hour SHIFT [12k, 12k+12) hours from mobilisation in which it attends anything at all, counted ONCE however many circuits it attends in it. APPORTIONMENT: divide each crew-shift between the circuits attended in it IN PROPORTION TO THE ATTENDED HOURS each took inside the shift; the share is a real number and is NOT rounded. A stage's attended hours are spread over the shifts its scheduled activities occupy IN PROPORTION TO THE HOURS of those activities in each shift, the same convention cl.3.9 uses for the daily water draw.
[Normal]      DURATION IS OCCUPIED TIME. A stage lasts as long as its activities OCCUPY: its duration is the SUM of the hours of the activities scheduled for it, and an idle gap between two of them is no part of it. No period this Section requires - a contact time, a circulation time, a displacement at the declared flow, a recirculation, a film-formation hold - is satisfied by an ENVELOPE that merely contains it. Work not done in the gap is not work done. The attended time of a stage is:
[Normal]        hydrostatic test        the specified hold
[Normal]        initial flush           n_f x V_f at the declared flow
[Normal]        chemical cleaning       the greater of the required circulation time and V_f at the declared flow
[Normal]        rinse                   n_r x V_f at the declared flow
[Normal]        passivation charge      V_f at the declared flow, plus the required recirculation
[Normal]        turnover                the fill volume of the declared method at the declared flow, plus the required recirculation
[Normal]      An unattended film-formation hold, and unattended standby inside a longer scheduled occupancy, are not charged (SW-01 cl.3, 01 91 13 cl.1.7); a stage with no attended time opens no shift. A crew attends one activity at a time and a rented unit serves one circuit at a time, so no crew may be charged with more than 12 attended hours in a shift and no unit held for more than 24 hours in a day.
[Normal]      WHAT a AND b MEAN FOR THE PROGRAMME. Both lines are bought by the period, so the two of them price the SEQUENCE, not the circuit: a programme that dovetails its circuits into the same unit-days and the same crew-shifts pays a fraction of what the same engineering costs when the circuits are run one after another. Neither line can be worked out from one circuit in isolation, and a circuit's share of both moves when another circuit's schedule moves. Against that pull stands cl.3.9 and SW-01 cl.2: the site's daily water allocation is shared too, so drawing the whole programme into a few days buys the excess at the trucked rate, and the cascade links of cl.3.6 force the circuits they join to rinse in sequence. The economic plan is the one that settles those against each other.
[Normal]   c. Water: metered rate up to the daily allocation and the trucked rate above it (SW-01 cl.1, cl.2). APPORTIONMENT: the allocation is a site-wide meter, so form ONE programme-wide average rate - the metered and trucked volumes priced at their own rates, divided by the total volume drawn - and apply that single rate to every circuit's draw. Do not attempt to attribute particular gallons to particular circuits.
[Normal]   d. Effluent: the sewer rate for volume to the metered connection, the tanker rate for volume removed from site (SW-03, RFI-031).
[Normal]   e. Chemicals: whole packages at the quoted package price (VD-06 Notes 1). ROUNDING: per dosing row - round each circuit's requirement for each product at each stage UP to a whole package. Do not pool a product's requirement across stages or across circuits before rounding.
[Normal]   f. EXCLUDED from the priced comparison, and to be provided by the Contractor within the lump-sum mobilisation: the hydrostatic test pump (the rented flush skids cannot reach the Section 23 21 16 cl.3.3 test pressure and are not intended to); any portable holding tank needed to move a cascaded displacement between tie-in locations; and the fine filtration any component's technical data requires at a pollution level the temporary strainer of VD-05 does not reach. These are scope and must appear in the Method of Procedure; they carry no price line and no bearing on the cost comparison.

[Title] SECTION 23 21 16 - HYDRONIC PIPING (EXCERPT)
[Normal] Tull Creek Data Hall - Issued for Construction, Rev 3, 2026-07-14
[Heading 2] 2.1   PIPE MATERIALS
[Normal] Carbon steel: ASTM A53 Grade B, Schedule 40, seamless, for sizes 2 in. and larger.
[Normal] Galvanized steel: ASTM A53 Grade B, Schedule 40, hot-dip galvanized after fabrication, for the makeup and fill riser only.
[Normal] Copper: ASTM B88 Type L drawn.
[Normal] Temporary flush hose: see VD-05.
[Heading 2] 2.2   ABSOLUTE ROUGHNESS FOR HYDRAULIC CALCULATION
[Normal] Use the following absolute roughness values, in feet, for all project hydraulic calculations:
[Normal]     Carbon steel, new                     0.00015
[Normal]     Galvanized steel, new                 0.0005
[Normal]     Copper, drawn                         0.000005
[Normal]     Temporary lay-flat flush hose         0.0008
[Heading 2] 2.4   PRESSURE RATINGS
[Normal] Permanent pipework, valves and fittings are rated for 300 psig at 200 degF.
[Normal] Temporary flush equipment, hose and strainers are rated as stated in VD-05 and VD-01/VD-02; the lowest rating in the assembled temporary circuit governs the test and flush pressure.
[Heading 2] 3.3   HYDROSTATIC TESTING
[Normal] Test each circuit hydrostatically at 1.5 times the system operating pressure of 85 psig, and in no case less than 125 psig, held for not less than 120 minutes with no loss of pressure and no visible leakage.
[Normal] The test pressure shall not exceed the lowest pressure rating of any component in the circuit under test, including temporary equipment.
[Normal] Circuits recorded as tested and accepted in CX-02 shall not be retested; retesting an accepted circuit is a change in scope. Any circuit not so recorded shall be tested before chemical cleaning begins.

[Title] SW-01 - CONSTRUCTION WATER AVAILABILITY MEMORANDUM
[Normal] Tull Creek Data Hall - General Contractor to Flush Contractor, 2026-07-02
[Heading 2] 1   METERED CONSTRUCTION WATER
[Normal] The site construction water meter is limited by the utility agreement to 62,000 gallons in any calendar day, for all trades. For the duration of the PCW flushing scope the whole of that allocation is assigned to this scope.
[Normal] Metered construction water is charged at $6.20 per 1,000 gallons.
[Heading 2] 2   TRUCKED WATER
[Normal] Additional potable water may be trucked in, up to 30,000 gallons in any calendar day, at $19.80 per 1,000 gallons delivered. Trucked water is of the same analysis as the metered supply (SW-02).
[Normal] THE LIMIT ON A DAY'S DRAW. Read the two paragraphs above together: the most water this scope may draw in any one calendar day is 92,000 gallons - the 62,000 gallon metered allocation PLUS the 30,000 gallon trucked entitlement. Drawing more than that in a day is not possible and no plan may schedule it. The metered allocation is NOT a limit on what may be drawn: it is where the PRICE changes. Volume above it in a day is bought at the trucked rate and is permitted, up to the trucked limit.
[Normal] Water drawn by an activity that spans midnight is counted against each calendar day in proportion to the hours of the activity that fall in that day.
[Heading 2] 3   FLUSH EQUIPMENT
[Normal] Three flush skids are AVAILABLE to this scope: two FS-600 units (FS-600-A, FS-600-B) and one FS-1200 unit (FS-1200-A). No further units are available, and no unit may serve two circuits at the same time.
[Normal] Availability is not hire. A unit is on hire only on a calendar day on which it is HELD - that is, a day on which some scheduled activity declaring it overlaps - and it is charged its day rate once for each such day, whatever work it does that day. A unit that is not held on a day is not charged for that day, and no unit is charged for the duration of the scope merely because it is available to it. Section 23 25 16 cl.3.10 a states how a day's hire is divided between the circuits that shared it.
[Normal] Commissioning crews are engaged by the shift, of 12 hours, at $820.00 per shift, and a shift in which a crew attends anything at all is charged whole. No more than 2 crews may be on the works at once.
[Normal] A unit serves one circuit at a time and a crew attends one activity at a time; the cost basis of 23 25 16 cl.3.10 divides each unit-day and each crew-shift between the circuits that shared it.

2 | Max Allowable Pressure Drop is the limit the component may be operated to at any flow, including temporary flushing flows.
3 | Pressure Rating is the component's maximum allowable working pressure and governs the hydrostatic test pressure of the circuit containing it, together with the rating of any temporary equipment in the assembled circuit.
4 | A component with a bypass provision is taken out of the flushed path by its temporary bypass spool; a component with none stays in the flushed path.

The Max Allowable figure shown for such a component is the mechanical rating of the casing or the vessel, not a flushing limit; it is recorded for completeness and no flushing flow this scope can produce approaches it. It is not a contradiction of the zero in the column to its left.
6 | Where a vendor data sheet quotes a pressure drop 'at the rated flow', that is the drop the component DEVELOPS at that flow and belongs in the Pressure Drop at Rated Flow column here. The Max Allowable Pressure Drop in this schedule governs (VD-03 note 5).

                 CHAPTER 6 CLOSED INDUSTRIAL WATER SYSTEMS

6-1           DEFINITION.

The term “closed water system” refers to a water system that is used to provide heating,
cooling, or both for industrial processes or facilities. The system is sealed (closed),
sometimes under pressure, and is not open to the atmosphere. No evaporation takes
place and, with good operation, water is lost only minimally from the system. In general,
water treatment for closed systems is much easier than for open systems. Makeup
water is needed only to replace seal leakage and other incidental leakage. Because of
the small makeup water requirements of these systems, they require little chemical
treatment, which can be added intermittently as needed. Once properly treated, the
system water does not form scale and has little or no corrosion potential. Two main
types of closed water systems are used at military installations: hot water closed heating
systems and chilled water closed cooling systems.

6-1.1         Hot Water Heating Systems.

Hot water heating systems are designed to produce hot water, and although they are
often referred to as hot water boilers, they are actually hot water heaters rather than
boilers. For new construction, hot water heating systems are preferred over steam
systems. Hot water heating systems, also known as hydronic heating systems,
recirculate water to distribute heat in facilities. They operate at three temperature
ranges:

        •     High-temperature water systems (pressurized systems with water
              temperatures higher than 350 F (177 C)) – no steam, only very hot water.
        •     Medium-temperature water systems (pressurized systems with water
              temperatures from 250 to 350 F (121 to 177 C)) – no steam, only quite
              hot water.
        •     Low-temperature water systems (water temperatures lower than 250 F
              (121 C))– no steam, only hot water.
6-1.1.1       Hot Water Boilers.

Hot water boilers can be either direct-fired (heated by combustion of gas, oil, or coal) or
unfired (heat supplied by steam from a steam boiler, heated by hot water from a higher-
temperature hot water system, or heated by a solar energy system). For many
applications, hot water boilers are preferred over steam boilers because there are
essentially no makeup water requirements and chemical treatment programs are less
complex and easier to maintain. They require less manpower for operation, less
maintenance, and have fewer water-related problems than steam boiler systems. Figure
6-1 shows a hot water boiler. Operate hot water boilers in accordance with UFC 3-430-
07 and UFC 3-430-11.




                                           149
                                                                              UFC 3-230-13
                                                                             1 March 2023

                                        Hot Water Boiler




6-1.1.2       Description of Hot Water Systems.

A typical hot water (hydronic) heating system is similar in composition to the closed
cooling water system shown in Figure 6-2, except that a fired or non-fired heat
exchanger is used rather than a chiller. Hot water boilers (fired and unfired) differ from
steam boilers described in Chapter 4 because hot water boilers:

       •      Provide heated water but do not generate steam.
       •      Do not have deaerating heaters. (These are not required because there is
              essentially no makeup water requirement and thus very little air enters the
              system.)
       •      Require recirculating pumps to distribute the heated water to the
              processing equipment.
       •      Require expansion tanks that contain a cushion of steam or nitrogen.
       •      Do not contain a condensate return because there is no steam generated,
              but there is a return system.
       •      Do not require blowdown.
       •      Are fabricated with mild steel components, but also may contain copper
              heat exchanger tubes, particularly in unfired systems.




                                            150
                                                                           UFC 3-230-13
                                                                          1 March 2023

6-1.2        Closed Chilled Water Systems, Brine Systems, and Glycol Systems.

Closed chilled water systems, brine systems, and glycol systems supply cold or chilled
water for cooling processes and air conditioning. They are water systems designed for
minimal loss of water. These systems contain mild steel piping, copper heat exchangers
and, in some systems, aluminum piping, stainless steel piping, cold rolled steel piping,
and potentially other metals.

6-1.2.1      Closed Chilled Water Systems.

Closed chilled water systems circulate water that is cooled by refrigeration equipment.
Water temperature ranges typically vary between 40 to 55° F (4 to 13° C). A typical
chilled water system is depicted in Figure 6-2. Chilled water systems can have large
storage capacity (1,000,000 gallons (3785 cubic meters) or higher). Chillers are shown
in Figure 6-3.

                     Typical Closed Chilled Water System Schematic




                                          151
                                                                            UFC 3-230-13
                                                                           1 March 2023

                                            Chillers




6-1.2.2      Closed Brine Systems.

Closed brine systems are chilled water systems in which calcium chloride, sodium
chloride, or a mixture of sodium chloride and calcium chloride has been added to the
water to lower its freezing point sufficiently to maintain it as a liquid (ice-free) at
temperatures of 30 to 50° F (-1 to 10° C). Brine systems have been largely replaced by
glycol systems.

6-1.2.3      Closed Glycol Systems.

Closed glycol systems are chilled water systems that contain a mixture of water and
glycol (ethylene or propylene) that will not freeze at the system operating temperature of
20 to 35° F (-7 to 2° C).

6-1.3        Combined Hot and Chilled Water Systems.

Some closed systems serve the dual purpose of producing circulating hot water during
the cold season and chilled water during the hot season.

6-1.4        Diesel Engine Jacket Cooling Systems.

Diesel engine cooling systems are considered closed systems, even when surge tanks
are open to the atmosphere.

The heat transfer from the circulating water is usually accomplished using a heat
exchanger, not by evaporation. These systems have low water losses. Several of the
metals used in these systems require good corrosion control. The three basic types of
diesel engine cooling systems are described below.


                                           152
                                                                          UFC 3-230-13
                                                                         1 March 2023

6-1.4.1      Air-Cooled Diesel Cooling Systems.

Air-cooled diesel cooling systems are used on most small engines as well as some large
engines. The jacket water is circulated through an air-cooled radiator. Antifreeze must
be used in these systems when radiators are exposed to low-temperature atmospheric
air or when the water temperature exceeds the boiling point (212° F (100° C))

6-1.4.2      Water-Cooled Diesel Engine Cooling Systems.

Water-cooled diesel engine cooling systems are used mainly on large engines. The
jacket cooling water passes through a heat exchanger, rather than a radiator, where a
separate cooling water loop removes the heat from the jacket cooling water. These
systems commonly use antifreeze.

6-1.4.3      Vapor-Phase Diesel Engine Cooling Systems.

Vapor-phase diesel engine cooling systems, also called ebullient systems, use water
that is heated to a temperature at the boiling point or above the boiling point for
pressurized systems. Steam is formed from the cooling water as it removes heat from
the system. The steam produced in this way can be recovered and used for space
heating. This type of system requires significant amounts of makeup water and
chemical treatment.

6-2          WATER TREATMENT FOR CLOSED SYSTEMS.

Water treatment programs for both closed hot water and closed chilled water systems
are developed primarily to control corrosion, although the programs may also control
deposition and microbiological organisms. If needed, scale deposition can be prevented
by external treatment (as with ion exchange softening) or can be controlled with
inhibitors as described in Chapter 4. Corrosion must be completely controlled by water
treatment programs. If corrosion occurs, corrosion products will eventually plug the
system, resulting in decreased operational efficiency and the need for cleaning.
Microbiological growth is not a concern in hot water systems, but can occur in chilled
water systems and should be controlled (see paragraph 6-2.3).

6-2.1        Makeup Water Requirements.

Makeup water requirements for closed systems are very small unless there are leaks in
the system (see paragraph 6-2.4). Closed systems should not be drained or purged
unless there is evidence that indicates the need to remove dirty water or sludge. For
proper operation, makeup water in high- temperature and medium-temperature water
systems is deaerated (de-oxygenated) using both mechanical and chemical methods
and is also softened. Oxygen can be removed from low-temperature water systems
either chemically or mechanically to prevent oxygen-induced corrosion. Chilled water
systems can require partial softening if the makeup water exceeds 250 ppm total
hardness (as CaCO3). The makeup water requirements are monitored carefully in
systems of all types (see Table 6-1). If there is an increase in the quantity of makeup

                                                                            1 March 2023

water required, the leak should be found and repaired quickly. After the repair, water
treatment chemicals should be replenished immediately.

6-2.2          Corrosion Control Programs.

Five basic water treatment programs are used in closed systems:
       •     Sulfite-caustic soda.
        •      Nitrite-azole.
        •      Molybdate-azole.
        •      Nitrite-molybdate-azole blend.
        •      Polysilicate-azole.
The choice of which chemical treatment system to use should be based primarily on the
water temperature and the metals in the system as well as the relative cost of the
treatment program at the specific installation. The various water treatment programs are
listed in Table 6-2 for each type of closed water system. Table 6-3 provides
microbiological control monitoring guidelines for closed water systems.

               Table 6-2 Selection Guidelines for Closed System Treatment

6-2.2.1        Sulfite-Caustic (or other Oxygen Scavenger-Caustic) Treatment
Program.

This program is required for high- and medium-temperature closed hot water systems. It
is optional for low-temperature water systems. The water is treated with sodium
hydroxide (caustic soda) and with sodium sulfite. This program is suitable for water
systems having temperatures up to 550 F (288 C). This chemical program is not
compatible with ethylene glycol nor propylene glycol. A recommended procedure for
maintenance is described below.

           1. Soften makeup water unless the total hardness in the makeup water supply
              is less than 10 ppm. The makeup water should be dealkalized if the
              makeup's total alkalinity is more than 200 ppm, as CaCO3.
           2. Add sodium sulfite to maintain 50 to 100 ppm sulfite (as SO3).
Add the appropriate chemical to maintain a pH of 9.0 to 10.0. A pH lower than 9.0 can
be raised by adding sodium hydroxide (caustic soda). A pH higher than 10.0 can be
lowered by adding sodium bisulfite.

           1. Test daily to maintain pH and sulfite levels within range.
           2. Deaerator can be used to help reduce incoming oxygen in high make-up
              systems.
6-2.2.2        Nitrite-Azole Treatment Program.

This program is not recommended for systems having water temperatures exceeding
250 F (121 C), or for (CL + SO4) concentrations>800ppm. Also, avoid nitrate-based
programs if (CL + SO4) concentrations is > 800ppm. It can be used in low-temperature
water and chilled water systems. Water is treated with a nitrite-borax compound to a
nitrite level of 1000 ppm (as NO2). This level will require about 1.7 to 1.8 pounds (0.77
to 0.81 kilogram) nitrite- borax per 100 gallons (0.38 cubic meters) of water in the
system. Most water treatment service companies offer this treatment as a formulated
product. There is also a generic nitrite-borax compound product that is a premixed
blend containing approximately 68 percent sodium nitrite, 10 percent borax, 17 percent
sodium carbonate (soda ash) and 5 percent copper corrosion inhibitor. Adjust to a pH of
9.0 to 9.5 with sodium carbonate (soda ash), if necessary. This chemical treatment
program is compatible with ethylene glycol water mixtures used for freeze protection. A
recommended procedure for maintenance is described below.

           1. Soften makeup water if the hardness is over 250 ppm as CaCO3.
                                            155
                                                                              UFC 3-230-13
                                                                             1 March 2023

          2. Add sodium nitrite-borax-azole blend to maintain a nitrite level of 600 to
             1000 ppm (as NO2) in the system.
          3. Add sodium carbonate, if necessary, to maintain a pH range of 8.5 to 9.5.
          4. If copper is present, maintain a minimum of 10 ppm of tolyltriazole.
          5. Test after chemical addition and then monthly for pH and nitrite levels.
6-2.2.3       Molybdate-Azole Treatment Program.

This program is not recommended for systems where water temperatures exceed
250 F (121 C). Most water treatment service companies offer this as a formulated
product. There is also a generic molybdate-azole compound product that is a pre-mixed
liquid containing approximately 10 percent sodium molybdate, 3 percent caustic soda,
and 3 percent azole (copper corrosion inhibitor). Maintain a molybdate level of 125 ppm
(as Mo) and adjust pH to the range of 8.5 to 9.5 with sodium hydroxide (caustic soda).
NOTE: Some restrictions may pertain to discharge of water containing molybdate. This
chemical treatment program is compatible with ethylene glycol or propylene glycol. A
recommended procedure for maintenance of the system consists of five steps:

          1. Soften makeup water if hardness is over 250 ppm as CaCO3 (calcium
             carbonate).
          2. Control the molybdate-azole compound to maintain a molybdate level of
             100 to 125 ppm (as Mo).
          3. Add sodium hydroxide (caustic soda) to maintain a pH of 8.5 to 9.5. It is
             likely that a buffer will be needed for pH control in this range.
          4. If copper is present, maintain a minimum of 10 ppm of tolyltriazole.
          5. Test monthly for proper pH and molybdate levels.
6-2.2.4       Molybdate-Nitrite-Azole Treatment Program.

This program is not recommended for use in systems in which water temperatures
exceed 250 F (121 C). An effective approach for corrosion control in these systems
involves a program that combines elements of the molybdate program and the nitrite
program. The targeted maintenance level for the combined addition of molybdate and
nitrite is about half of what either would be for individual addition. Most water treatment
service companies offer this chemical combination as a formulated product. This
chemical treatment program is also compatible with ethylene glycol or propylene glycol.
A recommended procedure for maintenance of the system consists of five steps:

          1. Soften makeup water if hardness is over 250 ppm as CaCO3 (calcium
             carbonate).
          2. Control the nitrite-molybdate-azole compound to maintain a nitrite level of
             300 to 400 ppm (as NO2), a molybdate level of 50 to 75 ppm (as Mo).
             Avoid this program if (CL + S O4) concentration exceeds [(NO2 + MO)-
             100]ppm.


                                            156
                                                                              UFC 3-230-13
                                                                             1 March 2023

          3. Add sodium hydroxide (caustic soda) to maintain a pH of 8.5 to 9.5. It is
             likely that a buffer will be needed for pH control in this range.
          4. If copper is present, maintain a minimum of 10 ppm of tolyltriazole.
          5. Test monthly for proper pH and treatment levels.
6-2.2.5       Polysilicate-Azole Treatment Program.

This program is not recommended for systems where water temperatures exceed
250 F (121 C). This program is especially beneficial when aluminum metal is present.
Aluminum is rarely found in comfort heating and cooling systems, but is sometimes
found in closed process cooling water loops or diesel engine jacket systems. Aluminum
will corrode at high pH, so the pH of the system water must be closely monitored if
aluminum is present. This chemical treatment program is also compatible with ethylene
glycol or propylene glycol. A recommended procedure for maintenance of the system
consists of five steps:

          1. Soften makeup water if hardness is over 250 ppm as CaCO3 (calcium
             carbonate).
          2. Control the treatment to maintain a polysilicate level of 80 to 100 ppm (as
             SiO2).Maintain a pH of 7.5 to 8.9. Adjust with dilute hydrochloric or caustic
             as necessary.
          3. If copper is present, maintain a minimum of 10 ppm of tolyltriazole.
          4. Test monthly for proper pH and treatment levels.
6-2.3         Treatment and Control of Microbiological Growth.

Treatment and control of microbiological growth is a concern in chilled or closed cooling
water systems. It is a particular concern if a nitrite-based corrosion inhibitor is used.
Nitrite can serve as a nutrient for some bacteria. Microbiocide selection must be
compatible with the corrosion inhibitor program and the pH levels in the system water.
Glutaraldehyde and isothiazolone are commonly used in chilled water systems.
Oxidizing biocides should not be used since they are not compatible with nitrite water
treatment.

6-2.4         Identifying Water Leaks.

The best way to check for leaks in a closed water system is to periodically read and
record the water usage displayed by a totalizing water meter installed in the makeup
water line or to use an inert, fluorescent material indicate a leak. The florescent material
can also be used to help pinpoint leaks or do leak studies. If the system does not have a
water meter, the existence of leaks can be checked by testing the inhibitor
concentration in the circulating water. The inhibitor concentration should be measured
once per month using molybdate, polysilicate, or azole, but not nitrite. Do not depend
upon the nitrite test; nitrite can be lost due to bacteria action. If nitrite is measured and
its concentration has decreased while the conductivity has remained constant, biological
contamination is present. If the measured values for both parameters decrease, there is
a leak in the system. Borate concentration would be the best indicator of leak detection.

                                            157
                                                                                                                                           UFC 3-230-13
                                                                                                                                          1 March 2023

When the inhibitor concentration has dropped to 98 percent of the original value, about
2 percent of the system water will have been lost. If the lapsed time for this 2 percent
loss is less than 4 months, the system's loss of water is excessive and any leaks should
be found and eliminated. Another convenient indication of water loss is the
measurement over time of a drop in conductivity. If the system water conductivity equals
that of the makeup, the treatment chemical is totally absent. Inert florescent material
can be added to the system and used to help pinpoint leaks, or do leak studies. Loss of
the fluorescent material can be monitored in real time; such loss indicates a leak.

NOTE: A 2 percent loss over 4 months equals 0.5 percent loss per month. The
accuracy of this test is limited, so if the loss for any month exceeds 1 percent, the test
should be repeated. If retesting confirms the water loss, the leaks should be found and
eliminated.

5-5.5.1         Effective Corrosion Control.

Effective corrosion control requires maintaining appropriate pH levels, plus adding
maintenance dosages of chemical corrosion inhibitors. Chemical corrosion inhibitors
form a protective film or barrier on the cooling system metal surfaces that have been
cleaned prior to adding an initial high dosage of inhibitor. The initial high dosage of
inhibitor passivates (protects) the metal. The appropriate dosage of corrosion inhibitor
must be maintained continuously in the cooling water to ensure continuing protection.
Table 5-11 shows examples of various passivation and maintenance dosage levels of
corrosion inhibitors. Corrosion inhibitors are divided into three classes: cathodic, anodic,
and general filmers. Corrosion inhibitors form a protective film on either the anode, the
cathode, or over the entire metal surface. The types of corrosion inhibitors are
described below.

5-5.5.1.1       Anodic Inhibitors.

Anodic inhibitors form a protective film coating on the anodic metal (where the metal is
lost) and thus directly control corrosion by preventing the reaction that results in
corrosion. Any unprotected areas will corrode at a much faster rate than the protected
areas, a factor that could result in pitting or localized attack of the unprotected areas.
Examples of anodic inhibitors include orthophosphate, nitrite, and orthosilicates. Under
certain conditions, molybdate can function as an anodic inhibitor.

                                               137
                                                                            UFC 3-230-13
                                                                           1 March 2023

5-5.5.1.2    Cathodic Inhibitors.

Cathodic inhibitors form a protective film coating of the cathodic metal (where metal is
not lost) and thus indirectly prevent corrosion by interfering with the current flow
required for the electrochemical reaction to proceed between the cathodic and anodic
metals. The corrosion reaction rate is governed by the size and type of the cathode
relative to the anode. Even when cathodic areas are not completely covered by the
protective film, corrosion will occur, but usually more slowly and uniformly than when
using anodic inhibitors alone. The occurrence of localized corrosion or pitting attack is
greatly reduced. Examples of cathodic inhibitors include zinc salts, polyphosphates, and
polysilicates. Under most conditions, molybdate will function as a cathodic inhibitor.

5-5.5.1.3    General Inhibitors.

General inhibitors produce a protective film on the surfaces of all metals. These
corrosion inhibitors are organic compounds, such as certain phosphonates, amines, and
other nitrogen chemicals. They may be used in cooling water systems.

5-5.5.1.4    Corrosion Inhibitors for Specific Metals.

Some corrosion inhibitors provide corrosion control for specific metals. The protection of
copper and copper alloys requires the use of azoles, such as tolyltriazole (TTA),
benzotriazole (BZT), and butylbenzo-thiazole, which can be added to the system
separately from, or as part of a blend of, other treatment chemicals.

5-5.5.1.5    Galvanic or Crevice Corrosion.

Control of galvanic or crevice corrosion is achieved primarily by engineering and
mechanical design. These types of corrosion can also be partially controlled by physical
and chemical considerations. A dielectric coupling (insulator), used to separate two
different metallurgies, can help to prevent galvanic corrosion. From a chemical
perspective, adjusting pH and using proper corrosion inhibitors will reduce corrosion.

5-5.5.1.6    Deposit Corrosion.

Control of deposit corrosion requires maintaining deposit-free metal surfaces. This
applies to any form of deposit, such as scale, biomass, corrosion products, or foulants.
The occurrence of most types of deposits is prevented by dispersants, scale inhibitors,
or biocides, along with the maintenance of adequate flow velocities. Routine, adequate
cleaning of filters and tower sumps will help reduce deposits.

5-5.5.1.7    MIC.

MIC is best prevented by stopping conditions that foster biological growth and by using
an effective microbiological control program. A MIC prevention program includes
adequate control (prevention) of deposits and fouling, avoidance of low-flow and dead-
leg conditions, and implementation of a consistently effective microbiological program
(see paragraph 5-4.4).

5-6      DEVELOPING AN EFFECTIVE COOLING WATER TREATMENT
PROGRAM.

An effective and complete cooling water treatment program addresses many factors,
including those associated with compliance and safety, protection of equipment, and
cost. Compliance and safety considerations are mandatory components of the program.
Achieving or exceeding minimally acceptable equipment protection at the lowest
possible cost is an advisable outcome for a well-designed program. The overall cost of
the treatment program includes not only the cost of chemical treatment, but also the
costs of water, disposal, manpower, and equipment. Development of an appropriate
cooling water treatment program is dependent upon knowledge of both the specific
equipment to be protected and the quality of the water to be used (source water and
system water).

5-6.1        Equipment.

Corrosion inhibitors are selected based on the metallurgy of individual pieces of cooling
system equipment. Typical systems include equipment components of different metals.
For example, systems may include smooth and enhanced copper tube bundles, mild
steel transfer piping, and galvanized cooling tower components; therefore, to select the
                                            139
                                                                               UFC 3-230-13
                                                                              1 March 2023

proper corrosion inhibitor, it is important to identify all metals contacted by the cooling
water. (See Table 5-10 for corrosion inhibitor selection criteria.)

5-6.2         Operational Features and Parameters.

Operational features and parameters of the cooling water system must be known to
select the proper scale and deposit inhibitors. This requirement refers to operational
parameters such as maximum temperature, minimum velocities, usage patterns, and
whether or not layup periods occur. The best chemical treatment programs cannot
overcome the stresses of poorly operated systems. A good example of system stress is
intermittent chiller operation that allows for SS accumulation (deposits) in chiller tube
surfaces due to low flow or lack of flow. This situation creates a strong potential for
under-deposit corrosion and for MIC that the chemical treatment may not be able to
overcome completely. Stagnant water can also cause deposits and corrosion. High
water temperatures can cause scale. The maximum water temperature should be
known so that the proper scale-control method can be used.

[5039 more lines in file. Use offset=6850 to continue.]

The term “stand-by” is often applied to a chiller that is in rotation with other chillers on-
line. This stand-by period could be of varying duration, from a few days to a few weeks.
Rotating chillers frequently is important for minimizing stagnant conditions that lead to
under-deposit and MIC corrosion. It is good practice to run the recirculation pumps
through a stand-by chiller for at least 15 minutes each day to minimize corrosion. A
chiller that must be left on stand-by for an extended period of weeks without
recirculation should be laid up wet or dry according to procedures described in
paragraph 5-7.4.

5-7.2         Common Problems during Layup or Due to Improper Initial Start-up.

Common problems that occur during layup or due to improper initial start-up include
corrosion of tubes and transfer piping (sometimes to the point of failure), micro-
biological growth with potential for MIC corrosion, and growth of pathogenic
microorganisms.

5-7.3         Start-up of New Cooling Water Tower Systems.

5-7.3.1       Initial Cleaning.

A new cooling water tower system will contain dirt, oils, greasy films, and rust located on
the metal surfaces as a result of system fabrication. A pre-operational alkaline cleaning
process is required to remove the dirt, oil, grease, and rust, and to prepare metal
surfaces for initial corrosion control. When galvanized steel is involved, special care
must be taken so that the pH does not exceed 8.5 during the cleaning and passivation
process to avoid conditions that promote white rust. The cleaning and passivating
procedure for a new cooling tower system is usually part of a new system construction
project and, as such, is not in the direct control of the cooling system operations
personnel. Verification of the completion of these important steps is obtained from the
contracting officer involved with the project. A cleaning and passivation procedure for
cooling tower systems with galvanized steel is provided below. The procedure is similar
for systems that do not contain galvanized steel, except that the pH restriction does not
apply.

5-7.3.2        Cleaning and Passivation Procedures.

In the startup of new cooling tower systems containing complex metallurgies that
include galvanized steel, follow the cleaning and passivation procedures for cooling
tower systems containing galvanized steel, stainless steel, mild steel, or copper. These
procedures should not be used for cleaning and passivating aluminum. Conventional
chemical cleaners and typical heating, ventilation, and air conditioning (HVAC) water
treatment programs use highly alkaline, high-pH water, which can initiate white rust
formation on galvanized surfaces and copper tubes. Galvanized steel can simply be
passivated by exposure to highly aerated water and a phosphate or polysilicate
treatment. This treatment forms a zinc corrosion inhibition layer, which is a natural,
dense, adherent, and protective corrosion product film. High pH (above 8.5) produces
unwanted white rust that is fragile and not protective against corrosion. The following
procedures are recommended.

5-7.3.2.1      Hydrostatic Testing.

Perform hydrostatic testing:

          a. Inspect and remove all debris.
          b. Fill the system with treated water and circulate. This should include
             orthophosphate or hexametaphosphate (as PO4) at 40 to 60 ppm, and
             tolyltriazole (active) at 10 to 20 ppm.
5-7.3.2.2      Pre-operational Cleaning Procedure.

If the system passes hydrostatic testing, proceed immediately to this pre-operational
cleaning and passivation procedure. Do not allow untreated water to be added to the
system.

          a. Drain and flush any debris from hydrostatic testing.
          b. Dose and circulate (for 24 hours) a sufficient amount of a cleaning formula
             based on the volume of the system. A formulation is provided below.
          c. Drain and flush the system, and clean all strainers.
          d. Fill the system with makeup water and circulate for 30 minutes.
          e. Take a sample of system water while it is circulating. The sample should
             match the makeup water supply for clarity and SS; conductivity ±10 percent;
             and pH ±0.3 pH units from 7.5 to 8.5.
If necessary, repeat steps a) through e) until the system water matches this description.
The system should now be clean and passivated.

5-7.3.2.3      Chemical Cleaning and Passivation Formulation.

Apply this chemical cleaning and passivation formulation when the water system pH is
7.5 to 8.5; adjust pH as required. Formulation limitations may require adding separate
components to keep things in solution. Other formulations may be used.

5-7.4.1        Wet Layup of Cooling Water Systems and Equipment.

Systems and system equipment such as heat exchangers, chiller tube bundles and the

Systems and equipment can be laid up dry, although dry layup is more appropriate for a
single piece of equipment, such as a chiller’s condenser tube bundle or other heat

acceptable. In humid climates you should use a desiccant such as a quicklime gel or an

5-3.6           Cooling Water Fouling.

The term “fouling” refers to the deposition of materials that are normally held in
suspension in the cooling water: mud, silt, and other SS brought into the system with
the makeup water; dust, dirt, and debris scrubbed out of the air passing through the
tower; product leakage such as oils; corrosion products from the system; and biological
organisms, both living and dead. Combinations of any or all of these materials can be
present in the cooling water.

5-3.7           Fouling Control.

Fouling from mud, dirt, and corrosion products can be controlled by the addition of a
water-soluble polymer dispersant, such as a polyacrylate. The addition of about 4 to 5
ppm of active polymer, together with sufficient water velocity (3.28 feet per second (1
meter per second)), can keep foulants in suspension and prevent them from being
deposited on heat transfer surfaces. Higher dosages (5 to 20 ppm) of active polymer
can be required for heavily fouled systems. It is best to reduce the loading of SS by
mechanically removing them from the system through blowdown, filtration, and physical
sump cleaning. Removing oil or oily materials requires a non-foaming surfactant.
Paragraph 5-4 describes prevention of fouling by biological organisms. Table 5-2
summarizes foulant control methods.

5-4             MICROBIOLOGICAL DEPOSITS AND CONTROL.

Microbiological organisms are composed of three classes: algae, bacteria, and fungus.
Large biological organisms such as clams, snails, mussels, or similar species are
referred to as macrobiological organisms. The presence of any biological growth can be
detrimental to cooling tower operations. Problems include fouling, corrosion, and loss of
efficiency.
